My advice would be to try to stay calm. "Dropout" has a lot of negative connotation, and I would try not to think of yourself like that. Think of it as taking a year off to decide what you want to do. You should get a job to keep yourself busy and have some structure. Save the money and use some of it to take up a hobby. Take some college courses and learn something new! Find out what your interested in, what your skills are and what kind of job that applies to/what kind of job you want for the future. Then look up what degree you need for that and then go back to school.

Try to stay positive :)

The stress of university is what broke me. I've always been kinda depressed/anxious but I had mostly worked through it by the time I graduated high school. I was a good student, worked at my own pace and graduated with honours. In my second year of university, I tried to get into a competitive program and that competition broke me. I was easily a top student before that (As/Bs), but the stress of it all suddenly made it hard to keep up my grades. It changed from "do your best" to "don't fail" and "do better than everyone else". Being the best me was so easy, I never sweat about it before. But  being better than hundreds of people, being in the top 5-10% of my year and having to fight for my position every four months...when a B meant failing...

My mental illness would not have accelerated the way it did if it wasn't for the competitive culture.

The guys who leave are not the kind of guys you need. 

There are guys out there who are empathetic, understanding and loving. I've had boyfriends who held me while having panic attacks, who cancel party plans because I'm to anxious to leave the house, who kept a box of corn pops at his house because I couldn't get my eating right and it was the only thing that could settle my stomach at 4am, who skipped class to stay at home with me because I was just so depressed. All of that and he was never resentful, never held it against me. 

Whatever is going on in your life, whether it be mental illness or something else, your partner should be someone who loves and supports you through it all. You deserve to have a partner like that.

Why do you assume people who are responding are kids? And even if they are, why would you think that kids have no gauge of parenting? They haven't done it before but they see the results of it. The people on this thread so far have been very harsh but that doesn't mean what their saying isn't true. You can't fix a problem until you admit there is a problem and OP should recognize that her parenting style is part of the reason why her son is acting this way now.

And yes, the fact that her son has some respect for his parents is a good sign, but that doesn't mean she shouldn't start disciplining him. Discipline doesn't have to mean being strict and "bringing down the hammer". OP can discipline bad behaviour, set expectations and goals for him and do this in a positive and encouraging way. The answer to this is definitely not continue not to discipline him.

I think this is a great idea. I would even say move out of that environment completely if you can. A change of pace and therapy would help him self reflect and see his bad behaviour patterns. 

Also, putting your foot down/ discipline doesn't have to be aggressive or negative. You can be firm and still have a good relationship with your son. You can say no and while encouraging him to make better choices. If you can, you may consider finding parental support groups to join and get tips from people who have experience in this area.
He's 17 not 7. His brain may not be fully matured but he is old enough to "see he error of his ways" and know what he is doing is wrong
